vignette: Naren, a 68-year-old South Asian man with a history of divorce and a current occupation in non-profit work, has been struggling significantly since his traumatic experience of being raped several months ago. His symptoms have profoundly affected his daily life and interpersonal relationships. The incident occurred one evening while Naren was returning home from a community event he had organized for his local non-profit organization. As he walked through the dimly lit alleyway that led to his apartment, a man approached him from behind and forcibly dragged him into an abandoned building where the rape took place. The trauma of this experience has left deep emotional and physical scars, shaping how Naren perceives his world today. In the immediate aftermath, Naren found himself struggling with intense feelings of vulnerability and helplessness. He began to engage in self-harm as a way to cope with these overwhelming emotions. The act provided him some temporary relief from the inner turmoil he felt but also reinforced his belief that he was not coping well. "My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper," he had come to believe. To mitigate feelings of isolation, Naren avoided being alone in a room or building at all costs. He would often seek out crowded spaces and stay up late watching television or engaging with neighbors to ensure he wasn’t by himself. This pattern led to significant disruptions in his sleep schedule and work performance. At the non-profit, colleagues noticed that Naren was increasingly absent from meetings and would arrive later than usual, which had strained his professional relationships. Naren’s heightened sense of threat manifested through his constant vigilance about sounds and touch. He would sit with his back against a wall to maintain visual control over his surroundings, ensuring he could see anyone approaching him. When someone touched him unexpectedly at work or during social gatherings, Naren reacted with alarm, often pulling away suddenly or becoming visibly anxious. "I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly," he explained. The intrusive memories were equally debilitating. At times, Naren would hear voices and sounds in his head that echoed those from the traumatic event. These auditory recall experiences left him feeling disoriented and on high alert for potential threats. He often checked to ensure no one was entering his home by listening for any unusual noises or footsteps outside his door. When memories of the rape resurfaced, Naren experienced physical pain in the same parts of his body where he had been hurt during the incident. "I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it," he said, describing how these vivid recollections left him feeling emotionally numb and detached from his surroundings. Naren’s negative appraisals compounded his struggles. He believed that he was permanently an outsider and would never be able to feel normal emotions again. "I will never be able to feel normal emotions again" echoed in his thoughts daily, reinforcing a sense of permanent detachment and isolation. Despite the pervasive impact on his life, Naren had managed to push through with minimal support until recently when his symptoms intensified. A particularly distressing incident at work where he was unexpectedly touched by a colleague triggered an intense emotional response, causing him to leave abruptly in the middle of a meeting. This episode marked a turning point for Naren, leading him to recognize that he needed professional help. Seeking therapy was a significant step for Naren, reflecting his desire to regain control over his life and emotions. While he remains deeply afraid of reliving the trauma and being judged, he hopes that with support, he can find ways to reconnect with his surroundings and feel less isolated. "I want to feel like I am not alone in this," he expressed during his initial session, highlighting both his fear and hope for a better future.
